strengths: Novel and timely extension of the function vector framework (Todd et al., 2024) from unimodal LLMs to a vision-language model (OpenFlamingo-4B), addressing a genuine gap since prior multimodal task-vector work (Hojel et al. 2024; Huang et al. 2024) has not targeted relational/spatial reasoning specifically.

The methodology is methodologically consistent with established causal mediation analysis (AIE) techniques, and the paper provides thorough ablations on injection layer, head-set size, and context size, which strengthen the mechanistic claims that a sparse subset of intermediate-layer attention heads carries relational information.
Experiments span both a controlled synthetic dataset (enabling precise causal analysis) and a more realistic dataset (GQA), which helps assess whether findings generalize beyond artificial stimuli.

The composite function vector experiment for one-shot analogy with untrained relations (e.g., above-left) is a genuinely interesting test of the linear representation hypothesis in a multimodal setting, and shows the approach outperforms few-shot ICL baselines even with more demonstrations.

Reasonable transparency: dataset construction is described in detail, a reproducibility statement promises code/data release, and limitations (single architecture, limited relation set) are honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The study relies entirely on a single, relatively small and dated backbone (OpenFlamingo-4B, a 3B-language-model-based VLM); it is unclear whether the localized, extractable-and-fine-tunable function vector structure generalizes to modern, more capable LMMs (e.g., LLaVA-family, Qwen-VL, InternVL), which substantially limits the significance of the central claims about how 'LMMs' encode relational knowledge.

Absolute accuracies remain quite low throughout (e.g., ~20-25% on synthetic relations and ~20-48% on GQA relations even after fine-tuning; ~16.8% on the analogy task), which, despite relative improvements over baselines, raises questions about the practical usefulness and robustness of the extracted vectors for real relational reasoning.

The real-image (GQA) dataset is very small (201 images total, 101 for training/extraction), and no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests accompany the many bar-chart comparisons in Figures 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, making it hard to assess whether reported differences are robust or due to noise/small-sample variance.

The comparison between fine-tuned function vectors (trained on up to 1000 zero-shot examples with a dedicated optimization procedure) and 4-shot ICL is somewhat asymmetric in terms of supervision signal used, which complicates the interpretation of 'fine-tuned FV significantly outperforms ICL baselines' as a fair apples-to-apples comparison.

No direct empirical comparison to existing multimodal task-vector methods (e.g., Multimodal Task Vectors, Visual Task Vectors) is provided, even though these are discussed as related work; this omission makes it difficult to situate the proposed approach's benefits relative to prior alternatives.

The scope of relations is narrow (four basic spatial relations plus four compositional variants), and hyperparameters such as injection layer (19 for synthetic, 8 for GQA) appear tuned per-dataset without a clear held-out validation protocol described, raising a mild risk of selection bias in reported results.
